title: IF GOSPEL WARRIOR EVER BECOMES ABOUT ME, THEN WE HAVE ALREADY LOST SIGHT OF JESUS.
paragraphs: IF GOSPEL WARRIOR EVER BECOMES ABOUT ME, THEN WE HAVE ALREADY LOST SIGHT OF JESUS.

This was never meant to build a man's name, defend a denomination, protect a religious institution, or win a cultural war. It was born from a conviction that the truth of Jesus Christ must never be buried beneath the very things people have built in His name.
There is something I need to say, even if it costs me followers.
Even if some people misunderstand me.
Even if those who once supported Gospel Warrior decide to walk away.
If Gospel Warrior ever becomes more important than Jesus Christ, I pray God will tear down everything in it that competes with His glory.
I mean that.
Because somewhere along the way, Christianity can become something frighteningly different from the faith Jesus taught.
We can become so consumed with defending our churches that we forget to love the people outside their doors.
So protective of our denominations that we treat fellow believers as enemies.
So attached to our traditions that we stop asking whether those traditions actually reflect Scripture.
So obsessed with political victories that we forget the Kingdom of God cannot be reduced to an election, a party, or a nation.
And so busy proving ourselves right that we no longer notice the wounded person standing in front of us.
The person Jesus would have stopped for.
The person we walked past while arguing about Him.
That should break our hearts.
Because what if we have spent years defending Christianity while slowly neglecting Christ?
What if the thing we call loyalty to God has sometimes been loyalty to our own religious identity?
What if the greatest threat to our spiritual lives is not always the world outside the Church, but the pride we have learned to disguise as righteousness?
I cannot ask those questions of others without first allowing them to confront me.
And perhaps that is where Gospel Warrior must always begin.
Not with a finger pointed at the world.
But with a heart surrendered before the cross.
Jesus once spoke words that should make every Christian leader, preacher, ministry founder, content creator, and believer tremble.
In Matthew 15:8–9, He rebuked religious hypocrisy by quoting Isaiah:
"Ὁ λαὸς οὗτος τοῖς χείλεσίν με τιμᾷ, ἡ δὲ καρδία αὐτῶν πόρρω ἀπέχει ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ."
The Greek communicates this devastating reality: This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far away from Me.
Jesus continued by confronting worship corrupted by human teachings presented as divine commands.
Think about that.
People can speak beautifully about God while their hearts remain distant from Him.
They can defend sacred customs while neglecting the One those customs are supposed to honor.
They can know religious language without knowing the humility of repentance.
They can win arguments about Jesus and still fail to resemble Him.
And before anyone uses those words as ammunition against another denomination, understand something.
That warning is for us, too.
For me.
For you.
For everyone who has ever mistaken being religious for being transformed.
I know how easy it is to become defensive when something we love is questioned.
Our church may have raised us.
Our traditions may remind us of our parents, our childhood, our most sacred memories.
Our community may have carried us through grief, poverty, sickness, and seasons when nobody else stood beside us.
Those things matter.
I am not asking anyone to despise their church, abandon Christian fellowship, or dishonor faithful spiritual leaders.
Scripture teaches believers to gather together, encourage one another, honor faithful leadership, and preserve the unity of the Spirit (Hebrews 10:24–25; Hebrews 13:17; Ephesians 4:3).
But there is a difference between loving the Church and treating a human institution as though it were incapable of error.
There is a difference between honoring tradition and placing tradition above God's Word.
There is a difference between being grateful for a pastor and surrendering to a personality cult.
There is a difference between defending biblical truth and defending our own pride.
And that difference matters eternally.
Because Jesus Christ did not die on the cross to make us loyal fans of religious personalities.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
He rose again to give life to those who believe in Him.
He calls us not merely to admire Him, but to follow Him.
And following Him sometimes means allowing His Word to challenge things we have believed our entire lives.
I remember the question that cuts through all the noise whenever I think about what Gospel Warrior is supposed to become.
If nobody knew who was behind this ministry, would the message still be worth sharing?
If my name disappeared, would Jesus still be proclaimed?
If every compliment stopped, would the work continue?
If the numbers fell, if the applause faded, if nobody thanked me, would the Gospel still be enough?
Those questions expose something deeply uncomfortable.
Because even ministry can become an altar where the human ego demands sacrifices.
A person can begin with a genuine desire to serve God and slowly become addicted to being recognized for serving Him.
The heart is capable of disguising ambition as calling.
And I never want Gospel Warrior to become another place where people are taught to admire the messenger more than the Messiah.
John the Baptist understood this danger long before social media, ministry brands, or online audiences existed.
When attention began moving toward Jesus, John did not fight to preserve his own influence.
He said something that should be written across the heart of every Christian ministry.
"ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι."
John 3:30.
"He must increase, but I must decrease."
The Greek verb αὐξάνειν (auxanein) means to increase or grow, while ἐλαττοῦσθαι (elattousthai) means to become less or decrease.
John was not describing a marketing strategy.
He was acknowledging the rightful supremacy of Christ.
That is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not that I must become famous.
Not that a page must become powerful.
Not that our community must defeat every other Christian community.
But that Jesus Christ must be seen more clearly, loved more deeply, obeyed more faithfully, and proclaimed more truthfully.
If Gospel Warrior grows while Christ becomes less visible, that is not success.
That is spiritual failure dressed in impressive numbers.
And there is another uncomfortable truth we must face.
Not everyone who disagrees with us is an enemy of God.
Some believers differ on secondary doctrines because they have inherited different theological traditions, studied different arguments, or sincerely understood certain passages differently.
Those disagreements should not be dismissed as meaningless. Truth matters. Doctrine matters. Some errors have serious consequences.
But neither should we pretend that every disagreement is proof of rebellion against Christ.
We must distinguish the essential Gospel from matters on which faithful Christians may disagree.
Paul confronted this very spirit of division in Corinth.
Some were identifying themselves with Paul. Others with Apollos. Others with Cephas.
The names were different, but the danger was familiar.
Religious loyalty was beginning to fracture a community that belonged to Christ.
Then Paul asked in 1 Corinthians 1:13:
"μεμέρισται ὁ Χριστός;"
"Is Christ divided?"
What a question.
A question that should silence our arrogance before it fuels another argument.
Christ is not a possession to be claimed by whichever group speaks the loudest.
He is Lord.
And His people are called to belong to Him.
That does not mean biblical doctrine is optional.
It means our doctrine must submit to the authority of Scripture rather than the demands of tribal loyalty.
It means we must test teachings carefully, as the Bereans did in Acts 17:11.
It means we must refuse false gospels, as Paul warned in Galatians 1:8–9.
It means we must speak the truth in love, as Ephesians 4:15 commands.
And it means that when Scripture corrects us, we do not have permission to protect our pride by silencing the correction.
Gospel Warrior will never be about pretending that all beliefs are equally true.
Jesus made exclusive claims about Himself.
In John 14:6, He declared Himself the way, the truth, and the life, and taught that no one comes to the Father except through Him.
The Greek word ἀλήθεια (alētheia) means truth.
Jesus was not presenting Himself as one religious preference among many.
He was revealing Himself as the definitive way to the Father.
But notice something.
The One who made that extraordinary claim also washed His disciples' feet.
The One who spoke with absolute authority also welcomed children.
The One who exposed hypocrisy also wept at a friend's tomb.
The One who never compromised holiness also received repentant sinners.
Truth without Christlike love becomes a weapon in proud hands. Love without truth becomes sentimentality without direction.
In Jesus, grace and truth are not enemies.
John 1:14 says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth.
In Greek, χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας (charitos kai alētheias).
Grace and truth.
Not grace instead of truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both perfectly embodied in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps this is why the story of the Samaritan woman in John 4 means so much to me.
She came to a well carrying more than an empty water jar.
She carried a complicated history.
Jesus knew about her five previous husbands and the man with whom she was then living.
The passage does not tell us every circumstance behind those relationships, so we should be careful not to invent motives or blame that Scripture itself does not assign.
But we know this.
Jesus saw the truth of her life.
And He did not turn away.
She raised the question of the proper place of worship, a dispute that divided Jews and Samaritans.
Jesus did not pretend their religious differences were irrelevant.
He said that salvation was from the Jews, and He pointed her toward a coming transformation in worship.
Then He spoke of those who would worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4:21–24).
In the Greek of John 4:24, we encounter the words:
"ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ"
En pneumati kai alētheia.
In spirit and truth.
Not a declaration that worship, doctrine, or community no longer matter.
Rather, a revelation that true worship cannot be confined to a rivalry between sacred locations. It must correspond to the nature and revelation of God.
And what happened next?
A woman whose life Jesus knew became a witness to the people around her.
She told them about the One she had encountered.
She did not need a religious empire.
She did not need a famous platform.
She pointed people toward Jesus.
And many believed.
That is the kind of witness I want Gospel Warrior to cultivate.
A witness that says, "Do not stop at me. Come and see Christ."
Because behind every screen is a person whose story we may never know.
A father working himself to exhaustion, wondering whether God still hears his prayers.
A mother who smiles in church but cries after everyone has gone to sleep.
A young believer quietly wrestling with questions they are afraid to ask.
A pastor who faithfully serves others while privately struggling with discouragement.
A person wounded by religious hypocrisy who now struggles to trust anyone speaking in God's name.
Someone who has committed sins they are deeply ashamed of.
Someone who has been told they are beyond forgiveness.
Someone who no longer attends church because the place that should have offered care became associated with pain.
And someone reading these words who has not prayed sincerely in months.
I do not know which story is yours.
But I know this.
You are not merely an engagement statistic.
You are not another number in a ministry report.
You are a human being made in the image of God.
And your soul matters more than the growth of this page.
That is why I refuse to believe Gospel Warrior should be measured only by followers, reach, reactions, or revenue.
Those things may help us understand how far a message travels.
But they cannot tell us whether a person has genuinely repented.
They cannot measure a restored marriage, a reconciled family, a conscience awakened by Scripture, or a heart learning to trust Christ again.
They cannot tell us whether someone closed their phone, opened their Bible, and prayed through tears for the first time in years.
And if one person is brought to sincere repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, that matters more than a million empty impressions.
Jesus Himself gave us the picture.
In Luke 15, He spoke about a shepherd who went after one lost sheep.
One.
Not because the other ninety-nine were worthless.
But because the lost one mattered.
And the same chapter gives us the story of a son who wasted his inheritance, disgraced himself, and eventually came to his senses.
When he returned, his father saw him from a distance and ran to meet him.
The son had rehearsed his confession.
He knew he had sinned.
He did not come home demanding that his choices be celebrated.
He came home acknowledging his unworthiness.
And the father welcomed him.
That is not a story about sin being harmless.
It is a story about mercy meeting repentance.
About a father whose compassion was greater than the son's expectation.
About restoration that the son could never have earned.
And ultimately, it points us toward the grace of God.
This is why our theme is not simply a slogan.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because He erases accountability.
Not because grace means consequences disappear.
But because through His death and resurrection, Jesus offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life to sinners who turn to Him in faith.
He does not call evil good.
He overcomes evil with a redemption we could never manufacture ourselves.
The cross is where the seriousness of sin and the greatness of divine love confront us together.
Romans 5:8 teaches that God demonstrated His love for us in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
Not after we perfected our religious image.
Not after we became respectable enough to impress the people around us.
While we were still sinners.
That is the Gospel.
And it is why no denomination, church institution, cultural identity, political movement, or ministry personality can take the place of Jesus Christ.
Churches can serve Him faithfully.
Traditions can help believers remember and practice biblical truth.
Cultures can express Christian worship in beautiful and varied ways.
Governments can protect justice and religious freedom.
But none of these can save a soul.
Only Christ saves.
And if we are serious about defending pure biblical teaching, then we must be just as serious about guarding our own hearts from the corruption of pride.
Because it is possible to defend the authority of Scripture while refusing to obey the passages that command humility.
It is possible to quote verses about holiness while ignoring verses about mercy.
It is possible to expose another person's sin while hiding our own.
Jesus warned about this in Matthew 7:3–5, when He spoke of someone noticing a speck in a brother's eye while failing to recognize the plank in their own.
He did not command us to abandon moral discernment.
He commanded us to begin with honest self-examination.
That is a warning I want Gospel Warrior to remember every single day.
Before we correct, we must be willing to be corrected.
Before we call others to repentance, we must remain repentant ourselves.
Before we speak about grace, we must remember how desperately we need it.
And before we claim to stand for Jesus, we must ask whether our conduct reflects His commands.
Some people will misunderstand this mission.
Some may assume that refusing denominational rivalry means refusing doctrine.
Others may assume that refusing political tribalism means Christians should never address public injustice.
Neither is true.
Scripture speaks to every area of life.
Christians should care about justice, the vulnerable, honesty, human dignity, and the moral consequences of public decisions.
But the Gospel must never be reduced to a party platform.
No political leader is our Messiah.
No nation is the Kingdom of God.
No culture has a monopoly on biblical faithfulness.
And no human movement deserves the unconditional allegiance that belongs to Jesus Christ alone.
Our citizenship in heaven, as Philippians 3:20 teaches, should shape how we live responsibly on earth without allowing earthly identities to become our ultimate hope.
Gospel Warrior is for the believer who wants Scripture to be examined carefully rather than used carelessly.
For the Christian who loves their local church but knows that every church must remain accountable to God's Word.
For the person who has been hurt by religion but is still willing to discover who Jesus truly is.
For the skeptic who asks difficult questions and deserves thoughtful, respectful answers.
For the struggling disciple who needs encouragement without flattery.
For the mature believer who knows that spiritual growth never ends with winning an argument.
For the person who has wandered far from God and wonders whether returning is still possible.
And for anyone who is willing to seek truth even when that truth confronts their most cherished assumptions.
Not everyone who reads Gospel Warrior will agree with every conclusion.
That is not a reason to stop searching Scripture together.
We can test claims, examine context, correct errors, and disagree without treating one another as disposable.
And where the Gospel itself is at stake, we must be willing to stand firmly, even when doing so is unpopular.
Because the aim is not unity at the expense of truth.
Nor truth used as an excuse for cruelty.
It is faithfulness to Jesus Christ.
There is something else I need to say about the future of Gospel Warrior.
A ministry that wants to reach more people requires real work.
Time spent studying Scripture.
Time spent examining historical context and biblical languages.
Time spent writing, editing, answering questions, preparing resources, and encouraging those who are struggling.
There are practical costs involved in producing and distributing resources.
And if God allows this work to reach more people, there may be opportunities to expand what we offer.
But I want to be absolutely clear.
The Gospel is not for sale.
God's forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Spiritual maturity cannot be bought.
A monthly payment does not make anyone more loved by Jesus.
We glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, worship, and lives surrendered to Him.
Supporting a faithful ministry can be one meaningful expression of that generosity.
But it is not the only one.
And it should never be confused with the price of God's favor.
Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that each person should give as they have decided in their heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which I want to invite support.
Not through fear.
Not through guilt.
Not by promising blessings that Scripture does not promise in exchange for money.
But through a transparent invitation to participate in work you genuinely believe is worth continuing.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, return to prayer, confront hidden sin, rediscover grace, or grow in your love for Jesus, I want you to know that you can help sustain and expand this work.

You may prayerfully consider it part of your broader Christian giving, an offering of support toward digital discipleship and Gospel-centered resources. But I would never ask you to neglect your family's needs, abandon your responsibilities to your local church, or replace biblical stewardship with loyalty to this page.
Not because merchandise is the mission.
It isn't.
The deeper purpose is to help people remain rooted in Christ.
And I want that purpose to remain visible in everything we do.
Resources intended to help believers study Scripture, deepen their understanding of the faith, strengthen their walk with Christ, and encourage others.
Free means free.
You do not have to purchase anything to be welcomed here.
You do not have to pay to hear that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
Not to build a kingdom around me.
But to help sustain a platform that must always point beyond me.
Perhaps your household is struggling.
Perhaps every peso, dollar, or whatever currency you earn is already committed to food, medicine, transportation, school expenses, or the needs of people depending on you.
Please hear me.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth in this community.
You can still be part of the mission.
You can pray.
You can study.
You can encourage someone.
You can share biblical truth with a person who needs it.
The old classmate you have not spoken to in years.
The relative who quietly stopped attending church.
The friend who has become bitter toward Christianity after watching religious hypocrisy.
The young person confused by competing voices claiming to speak for God.
The believer who has spent years trying to appear spiritually strong while privately falling apart.
What if one of them needs to hear that following Jesus is not the same thing as worshiping a denomination?
What if someone needs permission to examine the Scriptures without feeling disloyal to their family?
What if someone needs to remember that Jesus did not come merely to make sinners look respectable?
He came to save them.
Maybe sharing this will open a conversation you never expected.
Maybe it will not.
We cannot control how another person responds.
But we can faithfully make the truth available.
Not because these words deserve the authority of Scripture, but because the biblical passages we have considered deserve to be revisited.
Return to John 3.
Read John 4 slowly.
Study 1 Corinthians 1.
Meditate on Luke 15.
Examine Romans 5.
Do not simply take my word for what they mean.
Open your Bible.
Read the surrounding chapters.
Ask questions.
Test what is taught.
And where you find that I have misunderstood or mishandled Scripture, I would rather be corrected than applauded for being wrong.
That is how seriously I want us to take the truth.
And if you are willing, I want to ask you something deeply personal.
Not which denomination you belong to.
Not which pastor you follow.
Not which political party you support.
Not how many years you have been a Christian.
But this:
What is one thing you have had to surrender because following Jesus required you to choose His truth over your own pride, comfort, or religious assumptions?
You do not need to reveal private details or wounds you are not ready to share.
Perhaps your answer is, "I had to surrender my bitterness."
Perhaps it is, "I am learning to stop judging others."
Perhaps it is, "I have been defending my religion more than living my faith."
Perhaps it is simply, "Jesus, teach me to follow You."
And if you are in a season where you are struggling to hold on to faith, you can comment, "I'm still fighting."
Not as a performance for an audience.
But as an honest expression that you still want to keep turning toward Christ.
Let the comments become a place for thoughtful testimony, humble questions, encouragement, and prayer.
Not another battlefield where Christians compete to humiliate one another.
If you have been wounded by the Church, you deserve to be heard with compassion.
If you have questions about Scripture, you deserve more than dismissive slogans.
If you have fallen into sin, you need truth that calls you to repentance and grace that points you toward the Savior.
And if you have been walking faithfully with Jesus for decades, there is still room to grow in humility.
None of us has outgrown our need for Him.
Invite your family, your friends, your fellow believers, and even those who are skeptical of Christianity to follow and explore the message with us.
Not because we have every answer.
But because we are committed to seeking the answers under the authority of God's Word.
Your voluntary support can help sustain this work, expand its reach, and encourage the continued development of discipleship resources.
That you would know Jesus Christ.
Not merely know about Him.
Not merely inherit a religious identity.
Not merely memorize arguments against people who disagree with you.
But know Him through repentance and faith, walk in His truth, and grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior (2 Peter 3:18).
Because one day, the platforms we built will be gone.
The trends we chased will be forgotten.
The arguments that consumed so much of our attention will no longer matter in the ways we imagined.
The applause will fade.
Our earthly reputations will pass.
And all our ministry activity will stand beneath the searching judgment of God.
That thought should not drive us into despair.
It should drive us toward faithfulness.
Toward humility.
Toward the cross.
Toward the One whose name alone is worthy of our worship.
So if you ever see Gospel Warrior becoming a personality cult, challenge it.
If you ever see us placing human tradition above Scripture, question it.
If you ever see us using fear to pressure people into giving, reject it.
If you ever see us treating people as numbers instead of souls, remind us of what matters.
If you ever see us making the message about denominational superiority, political loyalty, or cultural pride instead of biblical faithfulness, call us back to Christ.
And if you ever see me becoming more concerned with defending myself than submitting to God's Word, pray that I will have the humility to repent.
Because I am not the Savior.
I am not the standard of truth.
I am not the head of the Church.
Jesus Christ is.
Colossians 1:18 declares that He is the head of the body, the Church, and that He is to have supremacy in everything.
Everything.
Including Gospel Warrior.
Including the person writing these words.
This is why the mission must remain bigger than any one person, while remaining entirely centered on one Person.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for our sins.
Risen from the dead.
Lord over all.
The One who receives the repentant.
The One who forgives the guilty.
The One who transforms lives through His grace.
The One who calls His people out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And the One who deserves all the glory.
If this ministry disappears tomorrow, I pray that whatever was faithful to Scripture will continue bearing fruit in the lives of those who encountered it.
If another faithful ministry reaches people we never could, I pray that we will rejoice.
If someone who once followed Gospel Warrior grows into a deeper walk with Christ through a local church or another trustworthy source of biblical teaching, I pray that we will celebrate.
Because we were never supposed to own people.
We were supposed to point them to Jesus.

And when the last article is written, the last video is watched, the last book is opened, and the last message is shared, I hope the testimony of Gospel Warrior will not be that we built something impressive.
I hope it will be that we remained faithful.
That we loved people enough to tell them the truth.
That we respected Scripture enough to be corrected by it.
That we proclaimed grace without excusing sin.
That we called people to repentance without forgetting our own need for mercy.
That we supported the Church without making an idol of institutions.
That we refused to turn Christ into a mascot for our earthly loyalties.
That we made room for the broken, the questioning, the repentant, and the weary to hear the Gospel.
And that through all of it, Jesus was lifted high.
Because this was never about making people say, "Look what Gospel Warrior has accomplished."
It was always about helping people say, "Look what Jesus Christ has done."
And if the world forgets who carried the message, but one wounded soul remembers the Savior, then the message was worth carrying.
